title: Noah Kim — hiring brain dump
content:
Quick summary:
- Candidate: Noah Kim (applied for Sr. Runtime Engineer)
- Interview date: 2025-02-11 (pair + system design + culture)
- My role: pair interviewer (Asha Patel) + short passback for loop
- High-level: strong systems intuition, pragmatic trade-offs, moderate gaps on quantization details and kernel-level performance tuning. Communicates clearly, good at structuring answers.

Signal and highlights:
- System design (45m): drew a clean multi-tenant inference architecture with autoscaling hints, warm pools, and fallback model variants. Emphasized SLO-driven routing and graceful degradation — good product sense.
- Pairing/code (40m): implemented a simplified KV-cache eviction sketch and reasoning about hot prefixes. Code smelled OK in interview context; used Python but referenced C++/CUDA trade-offs.
- Latency/cost thinking: repeatedly folded cost into decisions (batch sizing vs p99 tail). Mentioned using adaptive batching with latency budgets — aligns with Redwood's thesis.
- Communication: iterative clarifying questions, asked for success metrics early, summarized assumptions.

Gaps / concerns:
- Low-level performance: when pushed on fused attention kernels and memory layout specifics, answers were high-level; didn't cite specific kernel strategies (no experience with CUTLASS-like internals). Not definitive red flag but means ramp time on kernel tuning.
- Quantization: understands int8 benefits and accuracy trade-offs conceptually but hasn't deployed QAT/LLM quantization pipelines in prod.
- CI/ops hygiene examples were a bit thin — when asked about incident postmortems and rollback automation, described team processes but couldn't point to concrete systems they've implemented end-to-end.

Behavioral / culture fit:
- Role fit: comfortable in ambiguous, product-adjacent eng roles. Prefers cross-functional work (SRE + product) which fits our small runtime team culture.
- Collaboration: described mentoring junior engs and running brown-bag sessions — positive for org health.

Scorecard (0–5 scale where 5 is top):
- System design: 4
- Low-level performance / kernel dev: 2.5
- Coding: 3.5
- Debugging / production ops: 3
- Communication & collaboration: 4.5
- Overall recommendation: 3.5 (Proceed to deeper loop focusing on low-level perf + ops)

Bias calibration / caveats:
- Interviewer bias: I asked mostly infra and scaling questions; not much emphasis on model-family specifics. If other interviewers push heavily on quantization/kernels, score might drop.
- Late in loop: candidate mentioned sleep-deprived week; answers early in day were crisp, later sections slightly less sharp — maybe fatigue.

What I'd test next (recommended loop plan):
- Technical deep dive (pairing) focused on kernel/runtime performance: give a micro-benchmark and ask how they'd optimize memory layout and reduce kernel launches. Look for concrete kernel-level ideas (fusing, prefetching, workspace reuse).
- Ops scenario: run a simulated incident (p99 spike due to hot prefixes) — ask for mitigation steps and runbook changes.
- Short take-home: small quantization evaluation (profile a toy transformer and show throughput/quality numbers). This will reveal hands-on quantization experience.

Concrete action items / calendar:
- Ask Hiring Ops to schedule perf-deep-dive with Marcus (45m) and SRE ops scenario with Evelyn (30m) — target this week.
- Share high-level scorecard with hiring committee and attach this doc (HIR-2147).
- TODO: remind candidate to send a short sample of any perf/benchmarking artifacts (not required but helpful).

Open questions I flagged during interview:
- Which transformer families have they shipped with (LLAMA-like, Mistral, internal forks)? Candidate said mainly BERT/encoder and some decoder prototypes.
- Any direct experience with model parallelism frameworks (Megatron, FSDP)? Candidate mentioned familiarity but not production use.

Notes to self (unstaged):
- Be careful not to bias committee with my optimism around system design — their kernel gap matters for immediate needs.
- If we proceed, consider pairing them with a senior kernel engineer early in ramp to cover low-level gaps.

Raw quotes I liked:
- "I start designs with the SLO and work backwards to what the routing needs to do. If you get that wrong everything else is noise."
- "Batching is a health hazard for latency if you treat it as a knob rather than a constraint."

Bottom line summary (one-liner): solid systems+product thinker, needs hands-on kernel/quantization ramp — recommend continue but gate on kernel-focused follow-up loop.

-- Asha
